title: Prykarpattia
summary: Prykarpattia, also referred to as Subcarpathia, is a geographical region [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]] located at the northeastern foothills of the [[carpathians|Carpathian Mountains]]. It primarily encompasses Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast and parts of Lviv Oblast, forming a significant part of the historic region of [[galicia|Galicia]].

sections.heading: Historical Background
paragraphs: Prykarpattia was initially part of [[kievan-rus|Kievan Rus]]' and later became associated with the Principality of [[halych|Halych]], eventually integrating into the Kingdom of Poland.
Following the Partitions of Poland in 1772, the region came under the control of the Habsburg monarchy.

After World War I and the collapse of Austria-Hungary, Prykarpattia became contested territory between Poland and the short-lived [[west-ukrainian-peoples-republic|West Ukrainian People's Republic]], ultimately remaining part of Poland after the Polish-Soviet War.

With the 1939 invasion and partition of Poland by Nazi Germany and [[soviet-union|the Soviet Union]], the area was incorporated into the [[ukrainian-soviet-socialist-republic|Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic]], later falling under Nazi control until 1944. Today, it is part of [[modern-history-of-ukraine|modern Ukraine]], specifically the [[ivano-frankivsk-oblast|Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast]].

sections.heading: Geographical Features
paragraphs: Prykarpattia is often used interchangeably with the region of Pokuttya, although no official borders distinguish them. The term Prykarpattia generally refers to the entirety of Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, while Pokuttya is specifically associated with the eastern part of the same region.
Certain areas of southern [[lviv-oblast|Lviv Oblast]], including the cities of Stryi, [[truskavets|Truskavets]], and [[drohobych|Drohobych]], are sometimes considered part of Prykarpattia.

The [[dniester|Dnister River]] serves as the primary waterway in the region, with numerous smaller rivers flowing into it. Major urban centers in Prykarpattia include Halych, Kalush, and [[ivano-frankivsk|Ivano-Frankivsk]].

sections.heading: Cultural Significance
paragraphs: Prykarpattia is home to various [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] ethnic groups, including the [[hutsuls|Hutsuls]], Lemky, and Boyky, each contributing to the region's rich cultural tapestry.
